titleText.es: La Conjetura de Collatz Fuerte afirma que esto es cierto para cualquier conjunto de reglas aplicadas a mano de manera obsesiva.
titleText.en: The Strong Collatz Conjecture states that this holds for any set of obsessively-hand-applied rules.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official English title attributes are preserved exactly. The raster clips most of 53 at the left edge and most of 29 at the right edge; their values remain identifiable from the visible final digits and the printed Collatz arrows 53→160 and 29→88. OCR omitted the complete number diagram and missed the accent in DEJARÁN.

regions.labelEs: LA CONJETURA DE COLLATZ AFIRMA QUE SI TOMAS UN NÚMERO, Y SI ES PAR LO DIVIDES ENTRE DOS Y SI ES IMPAR LO MULTIPLICAS POR TRES Y LE SUMAS UNO, Y REPITES ESTE PROCEDIMIENTO DURANTE EL TIEMPO SUFICIENTE, AL FINAL TUS AMIGOS DEJARÁN DE LLAMARTE POR SI QUIERES TOMARTE ALGO.

excludedUnits.rationale: Collatz is the surname naming the conjecture, not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Si introduces a condition treated as real or possible, and tomas uses the ordinary present form for one familiar reader.
Si introduces the number-property condition, and es remains the ordinary present form.
Lo replaces the already named masculine number and stands before the changed verb divides.
Lo stands for the already named quantity, divides supplies the operation, entre introduces the number used to divide it, and dos is that number.
Si introduces the alternative number-property condition, and es remains the ordinary present form.
Lo replaces the already named masculine number and stands before the changed verb multiplicas.
Lo stands for the already named quantity, multiplicas supplies the operation, por introduces the number used to multiply it, and tres is that number.
Le identifies the value receiving the addition and stands before the changed verb sumas.
Le marks the current value as the receiver, sumas supplies the operation, and uno is the amount added.
Tiempo names the amount-like thing, and suficiente follows it to describe that the amount is enough.
Suficiente has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns here, while its plural form would be suficientes.
Al and final form the fixed expression meaning ‘in the end’ or ‘eventually.’
Dejar keeps its complete dictionary form and adds -án for what several people will do in the future.
Dejarán changes for several future actors, de is required, and llamarte remains an unchanged action verb with te attached.
The unchanged infinitive llamar carries te at its end to identify one familiar person being called.
Por si introduces the possible occasion, and quieres uses the ordinary present form.
Tomarse is learned with se; for one familiar person, te replaces se and attaches to the unchanged infinitive tomar.
Tomarte supplies the familiar-person form of the action, and algo completes the ordinary social invitation to have a drink or light bite.

cards.answerEn: conjecture; a mathematical claim not yet proved
cards.noteEn: A conjetura is a statement believed to be true but not yet proved. Outside mathematics it can also mean a reasoned guess.

example.es: La investigadora estudia una conjetura sobre números primos.
example.en: The researcher studies a conjecture about prime numbers.

cards.questionEn: What mathematical process is shown, and where does the joke come from?
cards.answerEn: It is the Collatz process: halve an even positive integer, or triple an odd one and add one, then repeat; the joke replaces a mathematical conclusion with friends eventually avoiding the obsessive hand calculation.
cards.noteEn: In the prompt, ÷ means divide, × means multiply, + means add, and the centered dots separate the main ideas. The Collatz conjecture says that repeatedly applying those two rules to any positive integer will eventually reach 1, though no general proof is known. The diagram traces many values into 1 while a person calculates by hand. The caption's final consequence is deliberately social rather than mathematical, and the title text extends the joke by calling obsessive manual use of any rules a ‘Strong Collatz Conjecture.’
De can join an invention, theorem, or named object to the person whose name it bears. English may instead use an adjective based on that name.

example.en: We study Newton's laws.

cards.noteEn: Afirma is a present form of afirmar for one person, document, theory, or other singular source. It introduces something presented as true.

example.es: El informe afirma que el método funciona.
example.en: The report states that the method works.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a real or possible condition with “if”?
cards.answerEn: Use si without an accent, followed by an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern treats the condition as genuinely possible. Spanish normally does not put a future-tense verb directly after si in this kind of condition; the result can appear separately as a statement, prediction, or command.

example.en: If you have time, call.

cards.noteEn: Tomas is the familiar singular present form of tomar. In a procedure, it can mean choosing or starting with a value or object.

example.es: Tomas un valor inicial y aplicas la regla.
example.en: You take an initial value and apply the rule.

cards.noteEn: For numbers, par means even. This is distinct from un par de, which means ‘a pair of’ or ‘a couple of.’

example.en: Twelve is an even number.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

example.en: The movie—we watched it yesterday.

cards.questionEn: How do you state a division operation in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Use dividir for the operation and entre before the number you divide by.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the pieces. Cantidad is the quantity being divided and may be named directly or replaced by lo or la. Divisor means the number you divide by. Only dividir changes for the person and time.

example.en: We divide fifteen by three.

cards.noteEn: Divides is the familiar singular present form of dividir. A preceding lo can stand for the number being divided.

example.en: You divide the total by four.

cards.noteEn: After dividir, entre introduces the number used as the divisor: dividir doce entre tres means ‘divide twelve by three.’ This differs from the location meaning ‘between’ or ‘among.’

example.en: Divide twenty by five.

cards.noteEn: For whole numbers, impar means odd: dividing it by two does not produce another whole number.

example.en: Nine is an odd number.

cards.questionEn: How do you state a multiplication operation in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Use multiplicar for the operation and por before the number you multiply by.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the pieces. Cantidad is the quantity being multiplied and may be named directly or replaced by lo or la. Factor means the number you multiply by. Only multiplicar changes for the person and time.

example.en: We multiply seven by four.

cards.noteEn: Multiplicas is the familiar singular present form of multiplicar. A preceding lo can stand for the value being multiplied.

example.en: You multiply the result by two.

cards.noteEn: After multiplicar, por introduces the factor: multiplicar cuatro por tres means ‘multiply four by three.’

example.en: Multiply six by five.

cards.answerEn: may have no separate English word; marks the thing receiving the effect
cards.noteEn: Le can appear before a verb even when a later phrase beginning with a names the receiver explicitly. English normally states that receiver only once.

example.es: Le cambié la rueda al coche.
example.en: I changed the car's wheel.

cards.promptEs: me/te/le/nos/os/les delante del verbo que cambia
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the short word that identifies who receives something?
cards.answerEn: Put me, te, le, nos, os, or les before the first verb that changes for the person and time.
cards.noteEn: The slashes in the prompt mean to choose the one receiver word that fits. A verb that changes for the person and time is often called a conjugated verb: estoy rather than the dictionary form estar. In a multiword verb phrase, the receiver word goes before that changed verb, so les estoy enviando places les before estoy, not between estoy and enviando.

example.en: I am sending them a photo.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an amount is added to an already identified value?
cards.answerEn: Put le before the changed form of sumar, then state the amount being added; an optional a phrase can clarify the receiving value.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the pieces. In the prompt, sumarle is the unchanged dictionary form sumar with le attached. When sumar changes for the person and time, le moves before it: le sumo, le sumas, le sumamos. The amount follows, and an optional phrase such as al resultado can name the receiving value.

example.en: We add one to the total.

cards.noteEn: Sumas is the familiar singular present form of sumar. With le before it, the small word can identify the value receiving the added amount.

example.en: You add two to the result.

cards.noteEn: Repites is the familiar singular present form of repetir. The e in the dictionary form changes to i in this present form.

example.en: You repeat the step until you finish.

cards.noteEn: Durante introduces a period of time. Natural English often uses ‘for’ before a measured duration, such as an hour, but ‘during’ before a named event or period, such as the meeting.

example.en: We waited for an hour.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Suficiente describes an adequate amount or degree. After neutral lo, lo suficiente means “enough” or “what is sufficient.”

example.en: That is enough.

cards.answerEn: in the; part of al final (“in the end”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “in the end” or “eventually”?
cards.noteEn: Al final can name the literal end of something or the eventual outcome after events have unfolded.

example.en: In the end, we decided to stay.

cards.noteEn: Dejarán is the plural future form of dejar. Before de plus an unchanged action verb, it means that several people will stop doing that action.

example.en: Soon they will stop calling.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, then de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form of a verb is called the infinitive. It usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only dejar changes to show who acts and when; the final verb stays in its dictionary form. Keep de in this pattern: dejar alone usually means “to leave” or “to let,” while dejar de + action means to stop doing that action.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone stops doing something?

example.en: I want to stop smoking.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; a required verb complement
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs require de before their complement or a following infinitive. English often absorbs this de into the verb’s translation: dejar de means “to stop doing,” while disfrutar de means “to enjoy.”

example.en: I stopped smoking.

cards.noteEn: Llamarte combines the unchanged verb llamar with te attached at the end. Te identifies one familiar person receiving the call.

example.en: I am going to call you tomorrow.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

example.en: I want to help you.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por si, 'in case'
cards.noteEn: Por combines with unaccented si before a possible event to form por si.

example.es: Lleva agua por si hace calor.
example.en: Take water in case it is hot.

cards.questionEn: How do you say 'in case' before a possible event?
cards.answerEn: Use por si, then an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: Si has no accent here. Even when the possible event lies in the future, Spanish normally uses a present-time form after por si: por si llueve, not a future form. The main clause names the precaution.

example.es: Lleva un abrigo por si hace frío.
example.en: Take a coat in case it is cold.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por si, 'in case'
cards.noteEn: Si remains unaccented in por si and introduces the uncertain event for which someone prepares.

example.es: Cierra la ventana por si llueve.
example.en: Close the window in case it rains.

cards.answerEn: to have; to get yourself (a drink or bite)
cards.noteEn: Tomarte is the familiar-person form of tomarse attached to the unchanged verb. Tomarse algo commonly means having a drink or light bite, especially as a social activity.

example.en: Do you want to have a coffee?

cards.questionEn: Where does me, te, se, nos, or os go when a verb used with one of those words stays in its dictionary form?
cards.answerEn: Attach the matching small word to the end: unir + me becomes unirme.
cards.noteEn: A pronominal verb is learned with se, such as unirse or acostarse. When its action verb remains in the unchanged dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, replace se with the form that matches the person and write it as part of the same word: acostarme, unirte, or irnos.

example.en: I want to go to bed early.

cards.questionEn: How can you casually suggest going for a drink or something to eat?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tomar followed by algo.
cards.noteEn: Literally, algo is ‘something,’ but tomar algo commonly means having a drink or a light bite in a social setting. The situation supplies what is consumed.

example.en: Do you want to get a drink after work?
